title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Marine
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: A cyberattack pushed all three North Carolina Ports facilities into manual processing — and the OT questions were never answered
items.content_text: The North Carolina State Ports Authority detected an unauthorised intrusion on 4 August and isolated core systems, causing a systems-wide outage that delayed gate opening at the Port of Wilmington, the Port of Morehead City and the Charlotte Inland Port. Cargo moved on manual processing while containment ran, and the Authority said normal schedules had been restored by Friday. It activated its cyber contingency plan and worked with NCDOT, the state Department of Information Technology and the US Coast Guard. No group has been named and the entry vector has not been disclosed. Worth saying plainly: the Authority did not state whether vessel operations, cargo-handling equipment or rail interchange were affected, so this cannot be read as either a confirmed OT compromise or a confirmed IT-only event. The instructive part is that a containment decision, not the attacker, is what closed the gate.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: North Carolina State Ports Authority statements — via CyberScoop and BleepingComputer
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Intrusion 4 Aug 2026; normal schedules restored by 7 Aug 2026

items.title: One 3PL compromise, eight idle European warehouses, and a customer list that keeps growing
items.content_text: Ceva Logistics, part of the CMA CGM group, was compromised on 29 July and told customers on 1 August. Eight European warehouses were affected and goods in them were not shipping, with knock-on delays reported for Bol, De Bijenkorf, ING, Ace & Tate, Ajax and Valve hardware buyers. Reporting on 17 August added Pokémon Center customers in the UK and Germany to the list of people whose personal data was potentially exposed — names, addresses, email addresses and phone numbers. Attribution is unresolved. For ports and terminal operators the lesson is the cascade rather than the breach: warehouse, transport and terminal systems exchange data automatically, so one third-party logistics provider going dark propagates into berth planning, yard utilisation and customer notification obligations within days.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Ceva Logistics customer notifications — via SecurityWeek and The Record
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Compromised 29 Jul 2026; customers notified 1 Aug; further data notifications 17 Aug 2026

items.title: Uber Freight says operations are normal after an extortion group claimed it stole dispatch and accounts-payable files
items.content_text: A group calling itself Helix claimed on 12 August that it had taken mailboxes, cloud storage, accounts-payable material and dispatch documents from Uber Freight, posting samples on a leak site; reporters could not immediately verify the files. Uber Freight said its systems were running normally and there was no effect on business operations, and it has not confirmed the scope or the entry route. Treat this as claimed, not confirmed. It is on this page because digital freight brokerage sits directly upstream of gate appointments, drayage scheduling and container pickup, and dispatch documents are exactly the material an attacker would use to make a convincing pickup or diversion request to a terminal.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Leak-site claim reported by TechCrunch; company statement via Reuters
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Claim posted and reported 12 Aug 2026 — unverified

items.title: CISA added the exploited vCenter flaw to KEV yesterday — 361 hosts compromised across 47 countries
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-59310, a path-traversal flaw in VMware vCenter Server, to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 August. Broadcom patched it on 29 July; exploitation began roughly five days later. German incident-response firm QUIRSO assesses with moderate confidence that a Chinese-speaking actor runs the campaign, counting around 361 affected addresses across 47 countries. The actor gains root on the vCenter appliance, plants a backdoor through cron and a reverse SSH binary, and in at least one case deployed Babuk-derived ransomware. Terminal operating systems, berth planning, gate and yard management and vessel-traffic displays are commonly virtualised on a single cluster ashore; if the management plane falls, every one of those services is reachable at once, which is precisely the scenario that forces a port into manual gate processing.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA KEV catalogue and QUIRSO research — via The Hacker News
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Patched 29 Jul 2026; exploitation from early Aug; added to KEV 18 Aug 2026

items.title: Medusa has passed 500 critical-infrastructure victims, and weaponises new bugs faster than most ports can schedule a patch
items.content_text: CISA and the FBI refreshed their #StopRansomware advisory on Medusa on 18 August. The cumulative victim count passed 500 critical-infrastructure organisations as of April 2026, up from roughly 300 in the March 2025 version — about 200 new victims in a year across healthcare, critical manufacturing, the defense industrial base, government facilities, IT and finance. The operational finding is the tempo: Medusa has been observed weaponising newly disclosed vulnerabilities within about 24 hours, and in some cases using exploits up to a week before public disclosure, because it buys them rather than developing them. Impact is enterprise-IT encryption plus data theft; no control-system involvement is alleged. For a port that is the whole point — encrypting gate, yard and documentation systems is enough to stop cargo without ever touching a PLC.

items.title: Gunra ransomware names transportation and logistics, and gets in through unpatched Fortinet devices
items.content_text: CISA, the FBI, NSA, DC3, the Secret Service and South Korea’s National Police Agency published #StopRansomware advisory AA26-222A on 10 August covering Gunra, a double-extortion operation built on leaked Conti source code that moved to a ransomware-as-a-service affiliate model this year. Transportation systems and logistics appear explicitly in the target list alongside utilities, critical manufacturing and government facilities. The initial access is the actionable part: affiliates exploit CVE-2024-55591 and CVE-2025-24472 in internet-facing FortiOS and FortiProxy — long-patched authentication bypasses that yield super-admin and defeat multi-factor authentication. The advisory ships indicators and detection content, so this is a hunt you can run this week rather than a research project.

items.title: Dragos counted 95 ransomware incidents at transport and logistics firms in Q2 — and none needed control-system access
items.content_text: Dragos recorded 1,140 ransomware incidents against industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, up 12 percent on the 1,020 in the first quarter. Transportation and logistics accounted for 95 of them, and firms that support industrial control environments — engineering houses, system integrators, equipment makers — for another 117. North America led with 514 incidents, and the United States alone with 431. The finding that matters for ports is Dragos’s central point: operators do not need access to control systems to stop production. Encrypting the IT that schedules, documents and bills the movement of cargo is sufficient, which is exactly the pattern seen at North Carolina Ports and at Ceva this month.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Dragos Industrial Ransomware Analysis, Q2 2026 — via Help Net Security

items.title: A CVSS 10.0 command injection gives unauthenticated root on Haiwell’s IoT Cloud HMI gateway
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-02 covers CVE-2026-19188, an OS command injection in the Haiwell IoT Cloud HMI Gateway rated 10.0. The Net Check feature reached through the /setting endpoint passes user input from the cmdPing Socket.io event to the operating system without sanitisation, allowing an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute commands as root. Version 3.40.1.12 is affected and Haiwell has published Scada-v3.50.1.19. Devices of this class appear across marine facilities in places procurement rarely tracks: shore power, bunkering skids, ballast and bilge monitoring, cold-store plant rooms at reefer terminals, and lock and bridge machinery. They are usually installed by a contractor, connected for remote monitoring, and never revisited.

items.title: SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced exposes Node-RED with no authentication — maximum-severity remote code execution
items.content_text: Siemens published ten advisories in its August Patch Tuesday round, the most severe being SSA-834709 for SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices running Industrial OS with Node-RED installed. The Node-RED HTTP interface enforces no authentication, so a remote unauthenticated attacker can reach programming nodes that execute system commands and run arbitrary code at maximum privilege. A fixed version is available. In marine settings IoT2050 gateways show up as protocol converters and data collectors between crane, conveyor, shore-power or terminal automation equipment and a monitoring platform — devices the control network trusts implicitly, commissioned by an integrator and then rarely patched.

items.title: A Windows IKE flaw went into CISA’s KEV catalogue with a three-day federal deadline — and IKE is what terminates ship-to-shore tunnels
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-33824, a double free in the Microsoft Windows IKE service extensions (IKEEXT) that leads to remote code execution, to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 August with a federal remediation deadline of 21 August. A three-day deadline is CISA’s signal that exploitation is active and broad. The marine relevance is direct: IKE and IPsec terminate the site-to-site links between head office, terminals and remote facilities, and the remote-access tunnels that crane and terminal-automation vendors, classification surveyors and shoreside support use to reach vessel and equipment networks. Code execution at the tunnel endpoint yields access that looks entirely legitimate in the logs, on the exact path that reaches operational equipment.

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Added to KEV 18 Aug 2026; federal remediation due 21 Aug 2026

items.title: CISA’s own OT monitoring suite needs patching — alongside the BMS and segmentation products that run terminal facilities
items.content_text: ICSA-26-230-01, published 18 August, covers six flaws in CISA Malcolm, the agency’s own open-source OT network traffic analysis suite — the most serious being CVE-2026-55676 at CVSS 8.8, an unrestricted file upload leading to arbitrary code execution, with fixes in releases 26.07.0 and 26.08.0 depending on the CVE. That matters more than the score suggests: Malcolm usually sits inside the OT network with a SPAN or TAP feed and broad visibility, so it is a high-value host wearing a monitoring badge. From the 13 August batch, two items belong on a terminal facility’s list: ICSA-26-225-14 for Johnson Controls Metasys (CVE-2026-34491, CVSS 8.0, persistent cross-site scripting that a low-privilege user can aim at an administrator, with versions 12 and 13 now end of support) and ICSA-26-225-03 for Johnson Controls Airwall, the zero-trust OT segmentation overlay, carrying a hardcoded cryptographic key and a path traversal, fixed in v4.1.0.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-230-01, ICSA-26-225-14 and ICSA-26-225-03

items.title: An MTSA waiver does not exempt you from the cyber rule, the Coast Guard has confirmed — and 16 July 2027 is the hard deadline
items.content_text: The Coast Guard clarified in late July that existing MTSA waivers do not exempt an operator from the Cybersecurity in the Marine Transportation System final rule — a point that had been read hopefully in some quarters. The rule took effect on 16 July 2025 and its personnel training milestone passed on 12 January 2026. The remaining obligation is the substantial one: by 16 July 2027, MTSA-regulated facilities, US-flagged vessels and Outer Continental Shelf facilities must have designated a cybersecurity officer in writing, completed a comprehensive cybersecurity assessment and submitted a cybersecurity plan for approval. That leaves under a year, and plan approval is not instantaneous. The North Carolina Ports incident, which the Coast Guard was engaged on, is a reminder that the reporting expectations apply well before the planning deadline does.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: USCG final rule (33 CFR) — compliance timeline summarised by Industrial Cyber and maritime counsel
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Rule effective 16 Jul 2025; waiver clarification 24 Jul 2026; full compliance 16 Jul 2027

items.title: A case for a federal cyber reinsurance backstop for US ports, built on concentration risk in terminal systems
items.content_text: The August issue of USNI Proceedings carries an argument for a federal port cyber catastrophe reinsurance programme, modelled on the terrorism risk insurance scheme: private insurers would keep writing primary cover while the federal government backstops catastrophic, systemic losses. The reasoning is concentration risk — a small number of terminal operating system vendors and cargo-handling OT platforms are used across many US ports, so one systemic event is correlated rather than isolated, and commercial policies frequently exclude state-backed attacks, with attribution disputes delaying recovery money when it is needed most. The author also proposes industry-wide standards and annual independent audits building on the Coast Guard rule. This is advocacy, not policy: nothing has been introduced or enacted.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: US Naval Institute Proceedings, August 2026 — opinion piece, limited free articles per month

items.title: The new national science and technology strategy names OT/ICS resilience and supply chains as priorities
items.content_text: The National Security Science and Technology Strategy, released today, sets out four pillars and names operational technology and industrial control system resilience, along with technology supply chains, as explicit priorities rather than sub-clauses of general cybersecurity. For marine operators the practical read is about funding and framing rather than obligation: nothing here is a requirement, no deadline attaches to it, and it changes nothing you must do this week. What it does do is give port authorities and fleet operators language that maps their OT programme to a stated national priority, which tends to matter when research funding, federal grant criteria and procurement standards are written in the following twelve months.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: National Security Science & Technology Strategy — White House, via Industrial Cyber
